newsitem.title: THAILAND: Fear pervades Cambodia, human rights group says.
newsitem.headline: Fear pervades Cambodia, human rights group says.

text.p: A climate of fear persists in Cambodia, more than a month after a bloody coup in the capital, and the international community must push to ensure that rights are respected, human rights observers said on Thursday.

"A month after the July 5-6 fighting, a climate of fear still prevails among the people," said Evelyn Serrano, head of a six-member human rights delegation that has just returned from a five day visit to Cambodia.

"Generally, people are afraid that the police and the military will come and loot their belongings, destroy their property and hurt or kill them as has happened to hundreds of households, shops and offices in Phnom Penh and in the countryside," she said.

The delegation of rights activists from five Southeast Asian nations met Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who launched the coup, and other senior officials in addition to U.N. representatives, victims and diplomats.

U.N. human rights workers estimate 40 people were killed after Hun Sen ousted his co-premier, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, on July 6. Most of the victims were believed to have been the prince's supporters, including several senior military officials and their bodyguards.

In the immediate aftermath of Ranariddh's ouster, government officials said one senior royalist official was executed after he was taken into custody and at least one was killed in the fighting. But the government denied any human rights abuses.
Scores of royalist politicians and supporters of Ranariddh fled Cambodia after Hun Sen's coup, including some 20 members of parliament. Others went into hiding.
Serrano said the international community needed to act now to take advantage of the fact that Hun Sen needed to gain international legitimacy.
"The role of the international community is very important now," she said.

"Based on our observations (Hun Sen) is very...preoccupied with consolidating his forces. So it is a very good opportunity for the international community to push, particularly for the respect of human rights, at this point because that would be a key factor in legitimising his government."

Serrano said Hun Sen had assured the delegation that he would respect human rights, and said his government was investigating to see how many people were killed during and after the fighting in Phnom Penh.

But Serrano said the delegation wanted an independent human rights commission to investigate and prosecute cases of human rights violations since the military and police who were investigating for Hun Sen were those accused of committing the abuses.
Hun Sen also said the government planned to normalise the situation and prepare for May 1998 elections.
"The election would be meaningless if it could not be held in a free and fair atmosphere. Cambodia is not a country like Myanmar (Burma)," Serrano quoted him as saying.
Burma's military rulers held a general election in 1990, but the government did not recognise the result when the opposition National League for Democracy swept the poll.
